metadata.disclaimer: OSA's own analysis of the CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1.2 against SP 800-53 Rev 5. CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1.2 is by the Center for Internet Security (CIS), published in March 2025 and licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. OSA uses CIS's safeguard numbers and implementation groups. The titles, pairs, rationale and gaps are OSA's own. Each clause is one of CIS's 153 safeguards. The coverage figure estimates how much of the safeguard the listed controls meet when put in place as written. Read CIS's text at cisecurity.org, and check each safeguard against it before you use this mapping for compliance or audit.

clause_group_titles.4: Secure configuration of devices and software

metadata.clause_titles_note: OSA's own short titles. The safeguard numbers and implementation groups are CIS's. CIS licenses its text CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and OSA publishes this mapping under CC BY-SA 4.0, so the titles, rationale and gaps are OSA's own words. clause_group_titles names the 18 CIS Controls in OSA's words, by CIS's number: safeguard CIS 6.3 sits in control 6.

clause_fields.implementation_group: CIS's implementation group for the safeguard: 1, 2 or 3, the first group that includes it. Each group takes in the one before, so a safeguard in group 1 is in all three. Group 1 is the base CIS sets for every organisation

edition_check.sources_note: CIS gives out its spreadsheet, change log and guide through a download form on its site. OSA downloaded them on 1 November 2026 and read the Navigator the same day.
edition_check.changes: CIS's change log sets the safeguards of v8.1 beside those of v8, and its v8.1 columns match the v8.1.2 spreadsheet word for word. Its glossary sheet has a column for v8.1.1 and v8.1.2, which rewords four definitions. Service Provider is shorter, with IT contractors, managed service providers and cloud service providers as its examples. Sensitive Data is framed by confidentiality, integrity and availability. Workforce names contractors where it named consultants, among those it excludes. Portable devices changes by one word. Beside the Navigator's v8.1 view, the v8.1.2 spreadsheet words the descriptions of 12 safeguards differently: 2.7, 5.1, 8.9, 11.1, 12.1, 12.2, 12.6, 16.2, 16.11, 17.2, 17.3 and 17.5. Three of those add substance. 11.1 asks for detailed backup procedures in the recovery process, 12.6 sets secure management protocols apart from secure communication protocols, and 17.5 gives relevant third parties a role in incident response. The others change a word or the punctuation. 8.4 and 9.4 sit in other asset classes, Network and Software. The numbers, titles and implementation groups are those of v8 and v8.1. The raters worked from the v8.1.2 text, so the mapping follows it.
edition_check.titles: The titles are now OSA's own short descriptions of the safeguards. Until this rebuild the file used CIS's titles. A script checks that each title shares at most three words in a row with CIS's title for the same safeguard. Row CIS 1.3, which repeated the title and pairs of 1.4, now describes 1.3.

clauses_edited.change: Now describes safeguard 1.3, the active discovery tool. Until this rebuild the row repeated the title and pairs of 1.4.

analysis.basis: OSA's own analysis, from CIS's text by three independent ratings. NIST's catalogue of registered crosswalks lists CIS's own mappings of the CIS Controls to the Cybersecurity Framework, the latest from v8.1 to CSF 2.0, posted on 23 December 2025. It has none to SP 800-53 (checked 1 November 2026). CIS publishes its own mapping to SP 800-53 under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, which allows it to be shared only unchanged and for non-commercial use. OSA's data is CC BY-SA 4.0, so OSA rated the safeguards itself and used none of CIS's mapping.

analysis.controls: SP 800-53 Rev 5.2.0 base controls, current ones only. An enhancement that addresses a safeguard counts for its base control, and the rationale names it. The multi-factor authentication safeguards, 6.3 to 6.5, concern the organisation's own users and list IA-02, whose enhancements ask for multi-factor authentication. 6.7 and 12.7 list IA-02 too. No safeguard asks for the authentication of customers or others outside the organisation, so OSA's rule for customer authentication changes no pair. Where NIST withdrew an enhancement and moved what it asked into another control, the raters named that control: central management of anti-malware, 10.6, lists PL-09, which took in SI-03(01). A family's policy and procedures control, the -01, is listed where the safeguard asks for a documented process: 4.1, 4.2, 7.1, 8.1, 11.1, 14.1, 15.2, 17.3 and 17.4.
analysis.method: Three AI raters each rated all 153 safeguards on their own, from CIS's spreadsheet of v8.1.2, with its guide to hand, and the control statements. None saw another's rating. OSA lists a control for a safeguard where at least two of the three named it. The coverage figure is the median of the three estimates of how much of the safeguard an organisation would meet by putting the listed controls in place. OSA wrote the titles, rationale and gaps after the controls were settled, from the raters' reasons and the gaps at least two of them named.
analysis.agreement_measure: The Jaccard index of each two ratings: the pairs both named, divided by the pairs either named.
analysis.coverage_agreement: The three coverage estimates for a safeguard lie within 10 points of each other for 134 of the 153 safeguards. The widest spread is 25 points, for 12.3.
analysis.pairs_note: The file lists 269 pairs over 100 controls, the 242 named by all three ratings and the 27 named by two. Every safeguard lists at least one control. 133 of the 153 list one or two, and 8.1 and 11.1 list the most, 4 each.
analysis.not_mapped: Every safeguard is mapped. CIS sorts its 153 safeguards into 18 controls and gives each safeguard its implementation group: 56 in group 1, 74 more in group 2 and 23 more in group 3. OSA maps the safeguards and names the controls in clause_group_titles. Until this rebuild the file also had a row for each control, CIS 1 to CIS 18, whose pairs had no recorded source.

clauses.title: Detailed inventory of enterprise assets
clauses.rationale: CM-08 asks for an accurate, complete inventory of system components, at the level of detail the organisation chooses, reviewed on a set cycle. CM-08(04) records who is accountable for each component.
clauses.gaps: CIS lists what to record for each asset, such as its addresses and owner, and asks for a review at least every six months. Choose those details and that cycle in CM-08. Include devices that connect regularly but sit outside the organisation's control.

clauses.title: Handling of unauthorised assets on the network
clauses.rationale: CM-07(09) keeps a list of approved hardware and stops anything else from being used or connected. CM-08(03) acts on an unauthorised component once it is found, for example by cutting its network access or isolating it.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to deal with unauthorised assets every week. Run CM-08(03)'s detection and response on that weekly cycle.

clauses.title: Active network scanning to find assets
clauses.rationale: CM-08(03) runs automated checks on a set schedule to find components on the network that lack authorisation. CM-08(02) keeps the inventory current by automated means, and an active scanner is one such means.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for active scanning of the network at least once a day. Make an active scanner one of CM-08's automated tools and run it daily.

clauses.title: DHCP lease logs as a source for the asset inventory
clauses.rationale: IA-03(03) standardises dynamic address leases and records each lease given to a device, which is what DHCP logging does. CM-08(02) keeps the inventory current from automated sources, and those lease records can feed it.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for the lease records to feed the asset inventory, with a check at least once a week. Link IA-03(03)'s records to CM-08's inventory on that cycle.

clauses.title: Passive discovery of assets from network traffic
clauses.rationale: CM-08(03) detects components on the network automatically and on a set cycle, which a passive listening tool can do. CM-08(02) uses those results to keep the inventory current.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a passive tool that finds assets by listening to network traffic. Add its findings to the inventory at least once a week, and count it among CM-08's automated means.

clauses.title: Inventory of installed software and licences
clauses.rationale: CM-08 counts installed software as a system component, so its inventory covers software at the detail the organisation chooses, reviewed on a set cycle. CM-10 tracks software held under quantity licences, which gives the licence count.
clauses.gaps: CIS lists the details to record for each piece of software, such as its business purpose, its publisher and the date it was first installed. Choose those details in CM-08.

clauses.title: Vendor support for authorised software
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) keeps a reviewed list of the software allowed to run, which is where the organisation marks supported software as authorised. SA-22 replaces components once vendor support ends, or arranges other support for any that have to stay.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a check of support status at least monthly. Treat software that has lost support as unauthorised, unless a recorded exception names its compensating measures and the risk accepted.

clauses.title: Removal or recorded exception for unauthorised software
clauses.rationale: CM-07 restricts software to what the organisation approves, and CM-07(01) reviews systems on a cycle and removes software found unnecessary or unsafe. CM-08(03) detects unauthorised software and sets off a defined response. CM-11 sets and enforces rules on what users may install, and monitors compliance.
clauses.gaps: CIS lets unauthorised software stay under a recorded exception, and asks for a review at least monthly. Record those exceptions, and set CM-07(01)'s review to that monthly cycle.

clauses.title: Automated discovery of installed software
clauses.rationale: CM-08(02) maintains the inventory, software included, with automated tools, so it stays current as installations change. CM-08(03) detects software components automatically and flags any that lack approval.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Application allowlisting
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) applies a deny-all, permit-by-exception rule, so only software on the approved list runs, and the organisation reviews that list on a set cycle. CM-07(02) stops programs running outside the organisation's rules.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the allowlist at least every six months. Set that cycle in CM-07(05).

clauses.title: Control of which libraries load into processes
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) uses a deny-all, permit-by-exception rule, so only listed software runs. Applied to libraries and modules, the same rule decides which code a running process may load.
clauses.gaps: CM-07(05) is written for programs. CIS applies allowlisting to the libraries a process loads as well. Extend the approved list to cover them.

clauses.title: Script allowlisting with signing and version control
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) lets only approved code run, and applied to scripts it blocks any that are unlisted. SI-07(15) authenticates code by its signature before it is installed, so the organisation can reject scripts that are unsigned or altered.
clauses.gaps: CIS takes allowlisting down to scripts and names version control as one way to enforce it. Extend CM-07(05)'s list to scripts, and keep the approved ones under version control.

clauses.title: Documented process for handling data throughout its life
clauses.rationale: RA-02 categorises the organisation's information by impact, which gives the process its sensitivity levels. SI-12 manages and retains information under legal and business requirements, which sets handling and retention limits. SI-12(03) sets how information is destroyed once its retention period ends.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for one documented process that names an owner for each set of data, reviewed every year. Gather the rules from RA-02 and SI-12 into that document.

clauses.title: Inventory of sensitive data
clauses.rationale: CM-12 records where chosen information is processed and stored, who can reach it and how its location changes. PM-05(01) keeps a current inventory of the systems that process personal data, one kind of sensitive data.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for an inventory that covers all sensitive data, with a review at least once a year that gives that data priority. Name the sensitive information types in CM-12 and set that cycle.

clauses.title: Need-to-know access permissions on data
clauses.rationale: AC-03 enforces approved authorisations for logical access to information, which is the job access control lists do. AC-06 limits each user to the access their duties need, which puts need to know into practice.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Minimum and maximum retention periods for data
clauses.rationale: SI-12 manages and retains information in line with the legal and operational requirements that apply to it. Those requirements set how long the organisation keeps each kind of data.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for both a minimum and a maximum retention period for each kind of data. Record both limits in SI-12's retention rules.

clauses.title: Disposal of data matched to its sensitivity
clauses.rationale: MP-06 sanitises media before disposal or reuse, with methods whose strength matches the security category of the information. SI-12(03) names the techniques for destroying or erasing information when its retention period is over.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Encryption of end-user devices holding sensitive data
clauses.rationale: AC-19(05) requires full-device or container encryption on mobile devices such as phones and tablets. SC-28(01) applies cryptography to information at rest on the components the organisation names, such as laptop and desktop disks.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Classification labels for the organisation's data
clauses.rationale: AC-16 defines the security attributes and values the organisation allows and binds them to information, which provides the labels. RA-02 categorises systems and the information they hold by impact and records the result, which gives the scheme its basis.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 categorises by impact level. CIS asks for an organisation-wide set of labels, such as public and confidential, reviewed every year. Define those labels in AC-16 and set the yearly review.

clauses.title: Map of data flows, service providers included
clauses.rationale: CA-03 documents each information exchange with other systems, service providers included, with its interface details and the impact level of the information. CA-09 does the same for internal connections and the information they carry. CM-13 maps how the system processes personal data and which components take part.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a record of all the organisation's data flows, provider flows included, reviewed every year. Bring these documents together and widen CM-13's map to data of every kind.

clauses.title: Encryption of removable media
clauses.rationale: SC-28(01) uses cryptography to protect stored information on the components and media the organisation names. Naming removable media in that list brings it into scope.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Encrypted transmission of sensitive data
clauses.rationale: SC-08 protects the confidentiality and integrity of information in transmission. SC-08(01) does it with cryptography, such as TLS or SSH, which prevents disclosure and detects any change along the way.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Encryption of sensitive data stored on servers
clauses.rationale: SC-28(01) applies cryptography to stored information on the components the organisation names, such as database and file servers. Listing the systems that hold sensitive data brings them into scope.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Segmentation of systems by data sensitivity
clauses.rationale: SC-07(21) and (29) isolate components and functions in separate subnetworks behind boundary protection. SC-32 partitions the system into separate physical or logical domains on criteria the organisation sets, such as data sensitivity.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for segments drawn by data sensitivity. Set sensitivity as SC-32's partitioning criterion, and keep sensitive data on the assets approved for it.

clauses.title: Data loss prevention tools that locate sensitive data
clauses.rationale: CM-12(01) uses automated tools to find chosen types of information on system components and keep its location records current. SC-07(10) prevents the unauthorised transfer of information out of the system, the protective side of a data loss prevention tool.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 scopes discovery to the organisation's own components. CIS extends it to data held at service providers. Feed what the tool finds into the data inventory.

clauses.title: Audit logging of access to sensitive data
clauses.rationale: AU-02 lets the organisation choose reading, changing and deleting sensitive data as event types to log. AU-12 generates audit records for those events on the components that hold the data.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a log of each access to sensitive data, changes and disposal included. Name those events in AU-02's list of event types to log.

clauses.title: Documented process for configuring assets and software securely
clauses.rationale: CM-01 sets out the process in documented configuration management policy and procedures, and reviews them on a set cycle and after set events. CM-02 keeps a documented baseline configuration under configuration control. CM-06 applies the most restrictive workable settings from common secure configurations and records approved deviations.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the process at least once a year. Set that cycle in CM-01.

clauses.title: Documented process for configuring network devices securely
clauses.rationale: CM-01 documents configuration management procedures that cover network devices as parts of the system, and reviews them on a set cycle. CM-02 keeps baseline configurations for network devices under configuration control. CM-06 sets hardened settings for those devices from common secure configurations.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the network device process at least once a year. Set that cycle in CM-01.

clauses.title: Screen lock after a period of inactivity
clauses.rationale: AC-11 locks the device after a period of inactivity that the organisation sets. The lock holds until the user authenticates again, which protects a session left unattended.
clauses.gaps: CIS caps the idle time at 15 minutes on general-purpose operating systems and 2 minutes on mobile devices. Set those limits in AC-11.

clauses.title: Host-based firewalls on servers
clauses.rationale: SC-07(12) puts host-based boundary protection, such as a host firewall, on the system components the organisation names. Naming servers there gives each one its own firewall.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Default-deny host firewalls for end-user devices
clauses.rationale: SC-07(12) adds host-based firewalls to the components the organisation names, such as workstations and laptops. SC-07(05) denies network traffic by default and allows it by exception, which gives those firewalls their default-deny rule.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Secure administration of assets and software
clauses.rationale: CM-02 holds configurations under configuration control, for example as code kept in version control. CM-07 prohibits or restricts insecure protocols, such as Telnet and plain HTTP for administration. SC-08 protects management sessions in transit, and SC-08(01) does so with cryptography, as SSH and HTTPS do.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Default accounts shipped with systems and software
clauses.rationale: AC-02 sets which account types are allowed and disables or removes the others, vendor default accounts among them. IA-05 requires default passwords and other authenticators to be changed before first use, which leaves any default account still in place unusable as shipped.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Removal of unneeded services and functions
clauses.rationale: CM-07 configures each system to provide only the capabilities it needs. CM-07(01) reviews systems on a set cycle, finds unneeded services and functions, and disables or removes them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Trusted DNS resolvers for assets and network devices
clauses.rationale: CM-06 makes the DNS resolver that each asset and network device uses a configuration setting, which the organisation chooses and enforces. SC-21 has resolvers check the origin and integrity of the DNS answers they receive, which is the protection a trusted DNS server gives.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to choose the DNS servers its assets and network devices use: its own or reputable public ones. Set that choice in CM-06.

clauses.title: Lockout after repeated failed sign-ins on portable devices
clauses.rationale: AC-07 limits consecutive failed logon attempts and locks the account or device automatically once a user goes past the limit, which the organisation sets.
clauses.gaps: CIS caps failed attempts at 20 on laptops and 10 on tablets and smartphones. Set those limits in AC-07.

clauses.title: Remote wipe of organisation data on portable devices
clauses.rationale: MP-06(08) gives the organisation the means to purge or wipe information remotely from devices it chooses. Choosing the portable end-user devices the organisation owns brings them within reach of a remote wipe.
clauses.gaps: CIS names the events that call for a wipe, such as a lost or stolen device or a person leaving the organisation. Set those events in MP-06(08).

clauses.title: Work and personal separation on mobile devices
clauses.rationale: AC-19 sets configuration requirements for mobile devices, and AC-19(05) protects organisation data inside a container on them. SC-50 enforces separation and policy in software between security domains, here the work and personal profiles.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a separate work profile on each mobile device that supports one, holding the organisation's apps and data apart from personal ones. Make that profile a configuration requirement under AC-19.

clauses.title: Register of every account in the organisation
clauses.rationale: AC-02 defines the account types in use and specifies the authorised users, roles and privileges for each account. It assigns account managers and reviews accounts against requirements on a set cycle.
clauses.gaps: CIS lists details to record, such as each holder's name, username, start and end dates and department. It also asks the organisation to confirm at least once a quarter that each active account is authorised. Record those details and set that cycle in AC-02.

clauses.title: Unique password for each asset, with minimum lengths
clauses.rationale: IA-05 requires authenticators strong enough for their use. IA-05(01) sets password rules, such as a minimum length and screening against weak passwords. IA-05(18) supports password managers, which make a different password for every asset practical.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a different password on every asset. It sets a minimum of 8 characters for accounts with multi-factor authentication and 14 for accounts that rely on a password alone. Add both rules to IA-05(01).

clauses.title: Deactivation of accounts after 45 days of inactivity
clauses.rationale: AC-02(03) disables accounts that stay inactive for longer than a period the organisation sets, which takes dormant accounts out of use.
clauses.gaps: CIS fixes the inactivity period at 45 days. Set that value in AC-02(03).

clauses.title: Separate accounts for administration and everyday work
clauses.rationale: AC-06(05) restricts privileged accounts to the named roles that need them. AC-06(02) has privileged users sign in with a non-privileged account for everyday work, such as web browsing and email.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Service account register with owner and purpose
clauses.rationale: AC-02 treats service accounts as one of the account types it manages. Each one has an assigned account manager and comes up for review on a set cycle.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a record of each service account's owning department, purpose and review date, and a review at least once a quarter. Record those details and set that cycle in AC-02.

clauses.title: Central directory for all accounts
clauses.rationale: AC-02(01) manages accounts with automated mechanisms, such as a directory service. IA-13 uses identity providers to manage identities, their attributes and access rights in one place.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Process for granting access when people join or change role
clauses.rationale: AC-02 requires approval before an account is created and grants access only on a valid authorisation. PS-05 reviews a person's access when they move to a new role and adjusts it to fit.
clauses.gaps: CIS prefers the granting process to be automated. Use AC-02(01) to automate account management where you can.

clauses.title: Process for revoking access when people leave or change role
clauses.rationale: AC-02 disables or removes accounts and alerts account managers when users leave or move, in step with personnel processes. PS-04 disables system access and revokes credentials within a set time of termination. PS-05 adjusts access to match the new role when a person transfers.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Multi-factor authentication for internet-facing applications
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) and (02) ask for multi-factor authentication on privileged and non-privileged accounts, which covers signing in to applications reachable from the internet. IA-02(10) provides single sign-on, which lets the organisation enforce it in one place.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 sets multi-factor authentication by type of account. CIS sets it by exposure: every internet-facing application that supports it, a third party's included.

clauses.title: Multi-factor authentication for remote access to the network
clauses.rationale: AC-17 sets connection requirements for each type of remote access and authorises each one before use. IA-02(01) and (02) ask for multi-factor authentication on privileged and non-privileged accounts, which covers remote connections. IA-02(06) adds the case where one factor comes from a separate device.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts
clauses.rationale: IA-02(01) requires multi-factor authentication for all access to privileged accounts. Administrator accounts are privileged accounts, so it applies to every one of them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Register of authentication and authorisation systems
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of system components with their details and reviews it on a set cycle. Authentication and authorisation servers are system components, so they appear in it.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a separate list of the systems that authenticate and authorise users, including those a service provider hosts. Keep that list yourself, starting from the CM-08 inventory.

clauses.title: Central access control through single sign-on
clauses.rationale: IA-02(10) provides single sign-on for the accounts and services the organisation chooses. IA-13 uses identity providers and authorisation servers to manage access rights and make access decisions in one place.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Role-based access rights with a yearly review
clauses.rationale: AC-02 sets the conditions for role membership and the privileges each account holds. AC-03(07) enforces a role-based access control policy. AC-06(07) reviews privileges on a set cycle, confirms each is still needed and removes the rest.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of privileges at least once a year. Set that cycle in AC-06(07).

clauses.title: Documented process for managing vulnerabilities
clauses.rationale: RA-01 documents the risk assessment policy and procedures, which cover vulnerability scanning, and reviews them on a set cycle. RA-05 sets out how the organisation scans for vulnerabilities and fixes them within the response times it chooses. SI-02 finds and corrects flaws as part of configuration management.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the process at least once a year. Set that cycle in RA-01.

clauses.title: Risk-based plan for fixing vulnerabilities
clauses.rationale: RA-05 sets response times for fixing confirmed vulnerabilities, based on the organisation's assessment of risk. SI-02 sets time frames for installing security updates. SI-02(03) measures how long fixes take against set benchmarks.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the remediation plan at least once a month. Set that cycle alongside the response times in RA-05.

clauses.title: Automated patching of operating systems
clauses.rationale: SI-02 sets a time limit for installing security updates. SI-02(04) brings in automated patch management tools, and SI-02(05) installs updates automatically on the components the organisation names, operating systems included.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for operating systems to be patched at least once a month. Set that time limit in SI-02.

clauses.title: Automated patching of applications
clauses.rationale: SI-02 sets a time limit for installing security updates, application updates among them. SI-02(04) brings in automated patch management tools, and SI-02(05) installs updates automatically on the applications the organisation names.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for applications to be patched at least once a month. Set that time limit in SI-02.

clauses.title: Vulnerability scanning of internal assets
clauses.rationale: RA-05 runs vulnerability scans across the organisation's systems at a frequency it sets. RA-05(05) grants the scanning tools privileged access, so they can also run authenticated scans.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for scans of internal assets at least once a quarter. Set that frequency in RA-05.

clauses.title: Vulnerability scanning of internet-facing assets
clauses.rationale: RA-05 scans systems and hosted applications for vulnerabilities at a frequency the organisation sets. Its scope includes the systems and applications that are reachable from the internet.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for scans of internet-facing assets at least once a month. Give those assets their own frequency in RA-05.

clauses.title: Fixes for detected software vulnerabilities
clauses.rationale: RA-05 sets the response times within which the organisation fixes confirmed vulnerabilities, based on risk. SI-02 corrects software flaws and installs security updates within a period the organisation sets.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to fix detected vulnerabilities at least once a month. Match the response times in RA-05 and SI-02 to that cycle.

clauses.title: Documented process for managing audit logs
clauses.rationale: AU-01 documents the audit and accountability policy and procedures and reviews them on a set cycle. AU-02 chooses which events to log and why, and reviews that choice. AU-06 decides how often audit records are reviewed and analysed. AU-11 sets how long they are retained.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the process at least once a year. Set that cycle in AU-01.

clauses.title: Audit logging turned on for every enterprise asset
clauses.rationale: AU-02 specifies which types of event each system must log. AU-12 turns on the generation of audit records for those events, across the system components the organisation names.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Enough storage capacity for audit logs
clauses.rationale: AU-04 allocates storage capacity for audit logs, sized to the organisation's retention requirements. Each logging destination then has room to keep its records for the full period the organisation sets.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Clock synchronisation with at least two time sources
clauses.rationale: SC-45 keeps the clocks of system components in step. SC-45(01) sets them by an authoritative time source, and SC-45(02) adds a secondary source in another region as a fallback.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Detailed audit records for assets holding sensitive data
clauses.rationale: AU-03 sets what each audit record shows. That includes the type of event, when and where it happened, its source, its outcome and the identities involved. AU-03(01) adds further detail, such as network addresses. AU-12 generates records with that content on the components the organisation chooses, such as those holding sensitive data.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Logging of DNS queries
clauses.rationale: AU-02 lets the organisation choose DNS queries as a type of event to log. AU-12 then generates audit records for those queries on DNS resolvers and the other components the organisation chooses.
clauses.gaps: CIS names DNS queries as an event to log, where an asset supports it. Add them to the event types you select in AU-02.

clauses.title: Logging of URL requests
clauses.rationale: AU-02 lets the organisation choose URL requests as a type of event to log. AU-12 then generates audit records for those requests on web proxies and similar components.
clauses.gaps: CIS names URL requests as an event to log, where an asset supports it. Add them to the event types you select in AU-02.

clauses.title: Logging of command-line activity
clauses.rationale: AU-02 lets the organisation choose command-line activity, such as shell commands, as a type of event to log. AU-12 then generates audit records for it on hosts and on terminals used for remote administration.
clauses.gaps: CIS names command-line activity as an event to log. Add it to the event types you select in AU-02, covering shells and remote administration sessions.

clauses.title: Central collection and storage of audit logs
clauses.rationale: AU-04(01) moves audit logs off the systems that produce them into separate storage. AU-06(04) reviews and analyses records from many components in one central place, as a security information and event management (SIEM) tool does. AU-12(01) compiles those records into a single audit trail, correlated by time.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Audit log retention for at least 90 days
clauses.rationale: AU-11 keeps audit records for a period the organisation sets, in line with its records retention policy. The organisation can choose a period of 90 days or more.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to hold audit logs for at least 90 days. Set that period in AU-11.

clauses.title: Review of audit logs for unusual activity
clauses.rationale: AU-06 reviews and analyses audit records at a frequency the organisation sets, looking for signs of unusual activity. It then reports the findings.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review at least once a week. Set that frequency in AU-06.

clauses.title: Audit logs from service providers
clauses.rationale: AU-16 coordinates audit information with outside organisations when it crosses organisational boundaries. SA-09 requires providers to apply the organisation's security controls and lets it monitor their compliance, for example through the logs they supply.
clauses.gaps: CIS gives examples of provider events to collect, such as sign-ins, user management and the creation or deletion of data. Name the event types you need in each provider agreement.

clauses.title: Latest supported versions of email clients and web browsers
clauses.rationale: CM-07(05) lets only approved software run, which limits users to the browsers and email clients the organisation allows. SA-22 replaces software once its vendor stops supporting it. SI-02 installs security updates within a set time, which keeps browsers and email clients on current versions.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: DNS filtering on every end-user device
clauses.rationale: SC-07 controls outbound traffic at managed interfaces, where a filter can refuse lookups of known malicious domains. SC-07(12) adds protection on each host, which carries that filtering to the device itself.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for DNS filtering on every end-user device, in the office or remote, to block domains known to be malicious. Enforce it on each device, so it keeps working away from the corporate network.

clauses.title: Network URL filtering for all enterprise assets
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces policy on where information may flow, so filters can block websites by category or reputation. SC-07 controls web traffic at managed interfaces, and SC-07(08) sends it through authenticated proxies where the filters apply.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for regular updates to the filters. Refresh the block lists and categories on a set schedule.

clauses.title: Limits on add-ons for web browsers and email clients
clauses.rationale: CM-07 limits software to the functions the organisation needs, which means removing or disabling unneeded add-ons. CM-11 sets rules on what users may install, extensions included, and enforces them.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Email sender authentication with DMARC
clauses.rationale: SC-08(01) uses cryptography to detect changes to messages in transit, which is what a DKIM signature does. SI-08 filters unwanted mail at its entry points, where receiving servers check a sender's SPF, DKIM and DMARC records.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to publish SPF, DKIM and a DMARC policy for its own domains, so that receivers can reject forged mail in its name. Publish them, and check them on inbound mail too.

clauses.title: File-type blocking at the email gateway
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces policy on information flows by type of content, so the email gateway can refuse unneeded attachment types. SI-03 places malicious code protection at entry points such as mail servers, where risky files are stopped.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for unneeded file types to be blocked at the email gateway. Decide which types the organisation needs, and block the rest there.

clauses.title: Attachment scanning and sandboxing on mail servers
clauses.rationale: SI-03 places malicious code protection at entry points such as mail servers, where it scans attachments as they arrive. SC-44 opens suspicious attachments in a detonation chamber, an isolated sandbox, to check them for malicious code.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Malware protection on every enterprise asset
clauses.rationale: SI-03 puts malicious code protection at system entry and exit points and on endpoints, where it detects and removes malware. It also keeps that protection running and up to date.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Automatic updates to malware signatures
clauses.rationale: SI-03 asks for malicious code protection that updates itself automatically as new releases appear. That keeps the signature files current on every asset the protection covers.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Autorun and autoplay blocked on removable media
clauses.rationale: CM-07 limits each system to the functions it needs and switches off the rest, such as running code automatically from inserted media. CM-07(02) prevents program execution under the organisation's rules, which can prohibit auto-execute features. MP-07 restricts how removable media are used on systems, through controls the organisation sets.
clauses.gaps: CIS names autorun and autoplay as the features to switch off. Add both to the functions CM-07 prohibits, for all removable media.

clauses.title: Automatic malware scans of removable media
clauses.rationale: SI-03 scans files from external sources in real time, as users open or run them on an endpoint. Removable media count among those external sources.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Exploit mitigations turned on in systems and software
clauses.rationale: SI-16 protects memory from unauthorised code execution, which is the job of data execution prevention and address space layout randomisation. SI-07 protects the integrity of system software, as operating system integrity protection does. SI-07(15) authenticates code before installation, as signed-app checks do.
clauses.gaps: CIS treats exploit mitigations as one group, to switch on wherever an asset or application supports them. SP 800-53 splits them between SI-16 and SI-07. Choose which to use on each platform.

clauses.title: Central administration of anti-malware tools
clauses.rationale: SI-03 provides the malicious code protection to be managed. PL-09 manages chosen controls from a central point. It took in central management of malicious code protection from SI-03(01), which NIST withdrew.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Behaviour-based malware detection
clauses.rationale: SI-03 lets the organisation choose non-signature-based mechanisms. SP 800-53 describes these as heuristics that detect malicious code by how it behaves, which is what behaviour-based anti-malware does.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Documented backup and recovery process
clauses.rationale: CP-01 asks for documented contingency planning policy and procedures, reviewed on a set cycle. CP-02 sets recovery objectives and restoration priorities in a contingency plan. CP-09 sets which user and system data to back up and how often, and protects the backups. CP-10 brings systems back to a known state within set times.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of the documented process at least once a year. Set that cycle in CP-01 and CP-02.

clauses.title: Automatic backups at least once a week
clauses.rationale: CP-09 backs up user-level and system-level information at regular intervals. The organisation chooses the interval to meet its recovery objectives.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for backups to run automatically, at least once a week, and more often for sensitive data. Automate them and set that frequency in CP-09.

clauses.title: Backups protected to the same standard as live data
clauses.rationale: CP-09 protects the confidentiality, integrity and availability of backups, and CP-09(08) encrypts them. CP-06 asks for an alternate storage site with controls equal to the primary site's. Backups held there get the same protection as the original data.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Isolated, versioned copy of backups
clauses.rationale: CP-06 keeps backups at an alternate storage site, and CP-06(01) places that site apart from the primary site. CP-09(03) stores backups of critical information in a separate facility or fire-rated container, away from the live system.
clauses.gaps: CIS's examples of an isolated copy use versioned backup destinations. Keep versioned copies in that isolated store, whether offline, in a cloud service or at another site.

clauses.title: Quarterly test restores from a sample of backups
clauses.rationale: CP-04 tests the contingency plan on a set cycle, recovery included, and acts on the results. CP-09(01) tests backups for reliability and integrity. CP-09(02) uses a sample of backup information to restore chosen functions during plan testing.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for test restores at least once a quarter. Set that frequency in CP-04 and CP-09(01).

clauses.title: Network infrastructure on current, supported software
clauses.rationale: SA-22 replaces network components and services once vendor support ends. SI-02 installs security-relevant software and firmware updates on network devices within a set time.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a review of network software versions at least once a month, to confirm each is still supported. Run that review as part of SA-22.

clauses.title: Secure network design and segmentation
clauses.rationale: PL-08 develops a security architecture, in step with the enterprise architecture, that shows how the organisation protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. SC-07 divides the network into subnetworks behind managed interfaces, arranged to fit that architecture.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for the network design itself to cover least privilege and availability. Write both into the network part of the PL-08 architecture.

clauses.title: Secure administration of network infrastructure
clauses.rationale: CM-02 keeps a current baseline configuration of network devices under configuration control. Infrastructure as code held in version control is one way to do that. SC-08 protects management traffic in transit, and SC-08(01) encrypts it, as SSH and HTTPS do.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Network architecture diagrams and documentation
clauses.rationale: PL-02 asks for a system security plan that describes the system's components and its connections to other systems, reviewed on a set cycle. PL-08 documents the security architecture and updates it as the enterprise architecture changes.
clauses.gaps: CIS centres the safeguard on diagrams of the network architecture. Draw them and keep them with the PL-02 plan and the PL-08 architecture.

clauses.title: Central network authentication, authorisation and accounting
clauses.rationale: IA-13 uses central identity providers and authorisation servers to make authentication and authorisation decisions. AU-12(01) compiles audit records from network components into one system-wide trail, which covers accounting.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for authentication, authorisation and accounting on the network to run centrally. Connect network devices and network access controls to the IA-13 services, and send their accounting records to the AU-12(01) trail.

clauses.title: Secure protocols for network access and Wi-Fi
clauses.rationale: IA-03 authenticates devices before they join the network, which is what 802.1X does. AC-18(01) protects wireless access with user or device authentication and encryption, as WPA2 Enterprise does. SC-08 protects the confidentiality and integrity of traffic in transit through secure protocols.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Remote access through a managed VPN and central sign-in
clauses.rationale: AC-17 sets usage rules for each type of remote access and authorises it before any connection. AC-17(02) encrypts remote sessions, as a VPN does, and AC-17(03) routes them through managed access control points. IA-02 authenticates organisational users through the organisation's sign-in services before they reach its resources.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Separate, segmented machines for administration
clauses.rationale: SC-02 separates system management functions from user functions, for example on separate computers. SC-07(15) routes privileged access through a dedicated managed interface, and SC-07(29) isolates chosen functions on their own subnetworks. SC-32(01) places privileged functions in separate physical domains.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for administrative machines to stay off the internet. Block their internet access with SC-07 boundary rules.

clauses.title: Central correlation and alerting for security events
clauses.rationale: AU-06(03) correlates audit records held in different places, and AU-06(04) brings them together for central review and analysis. SI-04(02) analyses events in near real time with automated tools, such as a SIEM. SI-04(05) raises alerts on signs of compromise, and SI-04(16) correlates monitoring data across the system.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Intrusion detection on hosts
clauses.rationale: SI-04 sets up monitoring across the system. SI-04(23) adds host-based monitoring on the components the organisation chooses, which is the job a host intrusion detection tool does.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Intrusion detection on the network
clauses.rationale: SI-04 places monitoring devices at strategic points across the network to watch for attacks. SI-04(01) connects the individual intrusion detection tools into one system-wide intrusion detection system.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Filtering traffic between internal network segments
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces approved information flows within the system and between connected systems. SC-07 monitors and controls traffic at key internal interfaces, such as the points where network segments meet.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Remote access based on device health
clauses.rationale: AC-17 sets configuration and connection requirements for each type of remote access, and authorises each type before anyone uses it. IA-03(04) bases device authentication on attestation of the device's configuration and state, which comes from the configuration management process.
clauses.gaps: CIS links how much access a device gets to its health: current anti-malware, a compliant configuration, and an up-to-date operating system and applications. Write these checks into AC-17's connection requirements, and confirm them through IA-03(04) attestation.

clauses.title: Network flow logs for review and alerting
clauses.rationale: AU-12 generates records on network components for the events the organisation selects, such as flow records. SI-04 collects monitoring data from across the network, and SI-04(04) watches inbound and outbound traffic for unusual activity.
clauses.gaps: CIS names the data to collect from network devices: flow logs, full traffic capture or both. Select that data as logged events in AU-12.

clauses.title: Intrusion prevention on hosts
clauses.rationale: SI-04(23) puts host-based monitoring on the components the organisation chooses. SI-04(07) acts automatically to stop suspicious events as soon as that monitoring finds them, which is what an intrusion prevention tool does.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Intrusion prevention on the network
clauses.rationale: SC-07 controls communications at managed interfaces, where inline devices can block malicious traffic. SI-04(04) monitors traffic entering and leaving the system, and SI-04(07) acts automatically to stop suspicious events.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Access control at network ports, such as 802.1X
clauses.rationale: IA-03 identifies and authenticates devices before they make a local or network connection, as 802.1X does at each network port. IA-03(01) makes that authentication cryptographic and two-way, for example with certificates.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Traffic filtering at the application layer
clauses.rationale: AC-04 enforces the organisation's flow policy on the content passing between systems, and AC-04(08) applies policy filters to that content. SC-07(08) routes traffic through proxy servers at managed interfaces, and SC-07(17) enforces the expected protocol formats.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Monthly tuning of security alert thresholds
clauses.rationale: SI-04(13) profiles common traffic and event patterns, then uses those profiles to tune monitoring devices. SI-04 also adjusts the level of monitoring when risk changes.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to tune its alert thresholds every month or more often. Add that cycle to the tuning SI-04(13) describes.

clauses.title: Security awareness programme for the workforce
clauses.rationale: AT-01 sets a documented policy and procedures for awareness and training, reviewed on a set cycle. AT-02 gives every user security literacy training when they join and at a set frequency after, and keeps the content up to date.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Awareness of phishing and other social engineering
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives every user security literacy training. AT-02(03) adds a topic on social engineering and social mining, teaching users to recognise an attempt and report it.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Password and multi-factor authentication training
clauses.rationale: AT-02 trains every user in the actions that keep systems secure, on topics the organisation sets. The course can cover multi-factor authentication, passwords and the care of credentials.
clauses.gaps: CIS makes good authentication practice a required training topic. Add it to the AT-02 course content.

clauses.title: Sensitive data handling and clear desk training
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives every user security literacy training on topics the organisation sets. Those topics can include the safe handling of sensitive data from storage to disposal, along with clear desk and clear screen habits.
clauses.gaps: CIS makes data handling a required training topic, clear desks and disposal included. Add it to the AT-02 course content.

clauses.title: Training on how data leaks by accident
clauses.rationale: AT-02 teaches every user the actions that protect information, on topics the organisation sets. The course can show the common ways data leaks by mistake, such as misdirected messages or lost devices.
clauses.gaps: CIS makes accidental data exposure a required training topic. Include it in the AT-02 course content.

clauses.title: Incident spotting and reporting for all staff
clauses.rationale: AT-02(04) teaches users to recognise suspicious messages and unusual system behaviour. IR-02 gives users incident response training matched to their role, which for most staff means spotting an incident and knowing whom to tell.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Staff reporting of missing updates and tool failures
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives every user security literacy training on the actions that keep systems secure, with topics the organisation sets. The course can teach staff to check that their devices are up to date and to tell IT when a security tool fails.
clauses.gaps: CIS makes missing updates and failed automated tools a required training topic, with staff telling IT about each failure. Add it to the AT-02 course content.

clauses.title: Training on insecure networks and home network setup
clauses.rationale: AT-02 gives every user security literacy training on topics the organisation sets. The course can cover the risks of working over untrusted networks and how to set up a home network securely.
clauses.gaps: CIS makes insecure networks a required training topic. Where staff work remotely, it adds guidance on securing their home networks. Include both in the AT-02 course content.

clauses.title: Security skills training matched to each role
clauses.rationale: AT-03 gives security training to the roles the organisation names, shaped to the work each role does. It runs before people gain access or take up their duties, and on a set cycle after that.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Register of service providers
clauses.rationale: SA-09 names the people who oversee each external service, which gives every provider an internal contact. PM-30(01) identifies and ranks the suppliers of critical systems and services.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a register of every known provider, with its classification and an internal contact, reviewed every year. Keep that register yourself, starting from SA-09's oversight roles.

clauses.title: Policy for managing service providers
clauses.rationale: SA-01 and SR-01 set documented policies and procedures for acquisition and for supply chain risk management, each reviewed on a set cycle. The acquisition policy in SA-01 covers the external services the organisation buys.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the policy to cover each stage of working with a provider, from classification and inventory through assessment and monitoring to decommissioning. Write those stages into the SA-01 and SR-01 policies.

clauses.title: Classification of service providers
clauses.rationale: PM-30(01) identifies the suppliers of critical systems and services and ranks them by priority. RA-03(01) assesses supply chain risk for systems and services and updates it as conditions change, which gives each provider a risk rating.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a classification scheme with factors such as data sensitivity, availability needs, regulation and risk. Define that scheme and classify each provider with it, drawing on the RA-03(01) risk ratings.

clauses.title: Security terms in contracts with service providers
clauses.rationale: SA-04 writes security requirements, and who is responsible for them, into acquisition contracts. SA-09 requires external service providers to meet the organisation's security requirements and to use the controls it names. SR-08 sets up agreements under which suppliers report compromises and share assessment results.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a yearly review of each provider contract to find missing security terms. Add that review, checking each contract against the SA-04 and SA-09 requirements.

clauses.title: Assessment of service providers
clauses.rationale: SA-09(01) assesses the risk before the organisation outsources a security service. SA-09 monitors each provider's compliance with the required controls on an ongoing basis. SR-06 assesses and reviews suppliers and the risks they bring on a set cycle.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Ongoing monitoring of service providers
clauses.rationale: SA-09 tracks each provider's compliance with the required controls on an ongoing basis, using methods the organisation chooses. SR-06 reassesses each supplier's risk on a set cycle.
clauses.gaps: CIS names sources to watch, such as the provider's release notes and the dark web. Add them to the methods SA-09 uses to monitor providers.

clauses.title: Secure exit from a service provider
clauses.rationale: AC-02 disables or removes accounts at the end of their use, including the user and service accounts linked to the provider. SR-12 disposes of the organisation's data and components by set methods, which can include data held on a provider's systems.
clauses.gaps: CIS treats leaving a provider as one process. Write an exit procedure for each provider that brings the account steps in AC-02 and the disposal steps in SR-12 together.

clauses.title: Secure development process for applications
clauses.rationale: SA-03 runs development under a life cycle that builds in security and assigns security roles. SA-15 asks for a documented development process that addresses security and names its standards and tools, with a review on a set cycle. SA-11 plans security testing and carries it out throughout development.
clauses.gaps: CIS also makes developer training and checks on third-party code part of the process. Add both to the process that SA-15 documents.

clauses.title: Intake and handling of reported software vulnerabilities
clauses.rationale: RA-05(11) gives outside parties a public channel to report vulnerabilities. SA-10 has the developer track security flaws through to resolution and report what it finds. SI-02 identifies and corrects flaws, and SI-02(03) measures the time each fix takes against set benchmarks.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a severity rating on each tracked vulnerability and a handling policy published for outside reporters. Rate each one in the tracking system and publish the policy.

clauses.title: Root cause analysis of vulnerabilities in code
clauses.rationale: SI-02(07) asks the organisation to analyse the root causes of flaws and act to remove them. It then checks that those actions dealt with the cause.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Software bill of materials for third-party components
clauses.rationale: CM-08 keeps an inventory of system components, at a level of detail that can include the third-party libraries built into the software. SR-04 documents where each component comes from and tracks its changes, which is what a software bill of materials records. SA-22 checks that each component still has support and replaces those whose support has ended.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the bill of materials to record the risk each component poses and to include components planned for future use. Review it at least monthly, and set that cycle in CM-08.

clauses.title: Current third-party libraries from trusted sources
clauses.rationale: SI-02 applies security updates, which keeps third-party components current. SR-04 tracks where each component comes from, and SR-04(03) checks that it is genuine and unaltered. SR-05(02) assesses each component before the organisation takes it on or updates it.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to prefer mature libraries and frameworks with a proven security record. Add that preference to the checks SR-05(02) makes before selection.

clauses.title: Severity scale and release threshold for application flaws
clauses.rationale: RA-05 scores the impact of each vulnerability with a standard measure and fixes vulnerabilities in order of risk. SA-15(01) sets quality metrics that each release must meet, and these can include a security threshold.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a minimum security level that code must reach before release. Set it among the SA-15(01) quality metrics, and review the rating system every year.

clauses.title: Hardened baselines for application infrastructure
clauses.rationale: CM-06 applies settings from common secure configurations, such as industry benchmarks, to servers, databases and similar components. It chooses the most restrictive settings that operations allow. CM-02 keeps those hardened settings as controlled baselines.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Production separated from non-production environments
clauses.rationale: CM-02(06) manages development and test baselines separately from the production baseline. CM-04(01) tests changes in a physically or logically separate environment before they reach production.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a standing separation between production and every non-production environment. Apply it to all non-production work, beyond the testing of changes.

clauses.title: Secure coding training for developers
clauses.rationale: AT-03 provides role-based security training on a set cycle. For developers, that means training in secure coding for the work they do.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Security principles built into application design
clauses.rationale: SA-08 applies security design principles, among them least privilege in SA-08(14), mediated access in SA-08(05) and secure defaults in SA-08(23). SI-10 checks each input for validity, such as its size and format. CM-07 limits each component to the ports and services it needs, which shrinks the attack surface.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Proven modules for security functions in applications
clauses.rationale: IA-13 relies on established identity providers and authorisation servers to handle identity and access. SC-13 uses the approved type of cryptography for each purpose, which keeps the application on accepted algorithms.
clauses.gaps: CIS also asks for audit logging and other security functions to come from vetted platform modules. Build them on the features the platform already provides.

clauses.title: Static and dynamic analysis of application code
clauses.rationale: SA-11(01) has developers run static code analysis during development and record the results. SA-11(08) adds dynamic code analysis, which tests the code as it runs.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Manual penetration testing of applications
clauses.rationale: CA-08 runs penetration tests on chosen systems, applications among them, at a set frequency. SA-11(05) has developers penetration test their own software at a depth the organisation sets.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Threat modelling of application designs
clauses.rationale: SA-11(02) has the developer carry out threat modelling during development. It pairs the threat model with an analysis of the system's vulnerabilities.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Named incident handling lead and backup
clauses.rationale: IR-08 asks for an incident response plan that assigns responsibility for incident response to named people or roles. That plan is where the organisation names who manages incident handling.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a lead and one or more backups, plus an internal overseer whenever a service provider handles incidents. Name them in the IR-08 plan and review the choice every year.

clauses.title: Contact list for incident notification
clauses.rationale: IR-06 reports incident information to the authorities the organisation names. That needs their contact details to hand. IR-08 asks for a plan that covers how incident information is shared and goes to named contacts.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for a contact list of the parties to inform, such as service providers, insurers, regulators and law enforcement. Keep it with the IR-08 plan and check each entry every year.

clauses.title: Incident reporting process for all staff
clauses.rationale: IR-06 has staff report suspected incidents to the incident response team within a time the organisation sets. IR-01 puts the incident response procedures in writing and reviews them on a set cycle.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the process to state the minimum details each report must contain. Publish the process where the whole workforce can find it.

clauses.title: Documented process for responding to incidents
clauses.rationale: IR-01 sets an incident response policy and procedures that cover roles and compliance, and reviews them on a set cycle. IR-08 adds an approved plan that sets out who does what and how information is shared, and keeps it up to date.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Incident response roles across business functions
clauses.rationale: IR-08 asks for a plan that describes how the incident response capability is organised. The plan assigns each responsibility to named people or roles.
clauses.gaps: CIS lists the business functions to involve, such as legal, human resources, public relations and facilities. Give each of them a role in the IR-08 plan.

clauses.title: Primary and backup channels for incident communication
clauses.rationale: IR-08 asks the incident response plan to cover how incident information is shared. SC-47 sets up alternate communication paths, so command and control carry on when an incident disrupts the usual ones.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to choose a primary and a secondary means of communication for incidents. Name both in the IR-08 plan and review them every year.

clauses.title: Incident response drills and simulations
clauses.rationale: IR-03 tests the incident response capability on a set cycle. IR-02(01) adds simulated events to incident response training, so staff practise their response.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for an exercise at least once a year. Set that frequency in IR-03.

clauses.title: Lessons learned after each incident
clauses.rationale: IR-04 feeds the lessons from each incident into the organisation's procedures, training and testing. It then makes the changes those lessons call for.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Criteria that separate events from incidents
clauses.rationale: IR-08 asks the incident response plan to define which incidents the organisation must report. That gives a starting point for separating events from incidents.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for written thresholds that tell a security event apart from an incident. Set them in the IR-08 plan and review them every year.

clauses.title: Penetration testing programme with defined scope and limits
clauses.rationale: CA-08 sets how often penetration tests run and what they cover, and CA-08(03) adds tests of physical facilities. CA-02 plans each assessment with its scope, procedures and roles, much as rules of engagement do for a penetration test.
clauses.gaps: CIS also asks the programme to set limits, such as attack types the testers must avoid, and to state what retrospectives it requires. Add both to the CA-02 assessment plan.

clauses.title: External penetration testing by specialists
clauses.rationale: CA-08 runs penetration tests on a set cycle, and CA-08(01) has an independent tester or team carry them out. RA-05(04) finds what an attacker could discover about the system, which covers the reconnaissance step.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for an external test at least once a year. Set that frequency in CA-08.

clauses.title: Prioritised fixes for penetration test results
clauses.rationale: CA-05 keeps a plan of action and milestones for the weaknesses that assessments find, and updates it as the fixes go in. RA-07 decides how to respond to each finding according to the organisation's risk tolerance.
clauses.gaps: SP 800-53 states this more generally than CIS. Check the controls against CIS's wording.

clauses.title: Defence review and detection tuning after penetration tests
clauses.rationale: CA-02 assesses whether controls work as intended, detective controls included. SI-04 adjusts monitoring as risk changes, and SI-04(09) tests the intrusion monitoring tools, so the organisation can tune detection after a test.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks the organisation to tune its detection rules after each test, where needed, so they catch the techniques the testers used. Add that step to every penetration test.

clauses.title: Internal penetration testing
clauses.rationale: CA-08 runs penetration tests on the systems the organisation chooses, internal ones among them. It also sets how often those tests take place.
clauses.gaps: CIS asks for an internal test at least once a year. Set that frequency in CA-08.
